title: Ibn Jubayr's Pilgrimage to Mecca and Back
intro: Ibn Jubayr, an Arab geographer, traveller and poet from al-Andalus, left Granada in 1183 to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. His travel chronicle describes Saladin's domains in Egypt and the Levant, which he passed through on the way, and Christian Sicily, which he crossed on the way home.
ending: He returned in 1185 by way of Sicily, after troubles that included a shipwreck. His chronicle became a foundation of the genre called Rihla, and later authors, among them Ibn Juzayy, copied passages from it.

stops.text: Ibn Jubayr, secretary to the Almohad governor of Granada, set out on the pilgrimage, accompanied by a physician from the city. He does not explain his reason for travelling.
stops.quote: He left Granada on 3 February 1183 accompanied by a physician from the city.

stops.text: He crossed the Strait of Gibraltar to Ceuta, then under Muslim rule, and boarded a Genoese ship bound for Alexandria.
stops.quote: He boarded a Genoese ship on February 24, 1183 and set sail for Alexandria.

stops.text: The ship passed the Balearic Islands and sailed off the west coast of Sardinia. There Ibn Jubayr heard of 80 Muslim men, women and children abducted from North Africa and being sold into slavery.
stops.quote: His sea journey took him past the Balearic Islands and then across to the west coast of Sardinia. Offshore, he heard of the fate of 80 Muslim men, women and children who had been abducted from North Africa and were being sold into slavery.

stops.text: A severe storm struck between Sardinia and Sicily before the ship reached Alexandria. There customs officials took zakat from the pilgrims, and Ibn Jubayr saw the Lighthouse of Alexandria, then still standing. He stayed eight days.
stops.quote: He arrived in Alexandria on March 26.

stops.text: He visited the cemetery at al-Qarafah and saw the citadel walls being extended under Saladin, a bridge over the Nile being built, a free hospital, the pyramids and the Sphinx.
stops.quote: He reached Cairo three days later. In the city, he visited the cemetery at al-Qarafah, which contained the graves of many important figures in the history of Islam.

stops.text: Ibn Jubayr spent 32 days in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, a Crusader state. Thirteen of them were spent anchored in the port of Acre, awaiting a favourable wind.
stops.quote: Thirteen of these days were spent anchored in the port of Acre, awaiting a favorable wind.

stops.text: Late in his travels, at the close of night, he saw the red flame of the volcano Stromboli throwing tongues of fire into the air.
stops.quote: In Sicily, at the very late stages of his travels (December 1184 to January 1185), Ibn Jubayr recounted other experiences. He commented on the activity of the volcanoes:

stops.text: He described Palermo as the metropolis of the island, an ancient city built in the Cordova style of cut stone. He noted that its Christian women followed the fashion of Muslim women.
stops.quote: It is the metropolis of these islands, combining the benefits of wealth and splendor, and having all that you could wish of beauty, real or apparent, and all the needs of subsistence, mature and fresh.

notes: The article gives the route only in part. It names Medina, Mecca, Damascus, Mosul, Acre and Baghdad without order, dates or events, and Basra only for Indian timber in ships, so those are left out (Mecca and Medina, the goal, included). Tibnin is named without date or place in the order, so left out. Acre is placed after Cairo and before Sicily because the article has him return in 1185 by way of Sicily, but it does not state the order; its year 1184 is inferred (the article gives no date for the stay). Cairo's date is only 'three days' after eight days at Alexandria, so the year 1183 is inferred. The Cairo and Acre quotes carry the place and the event. Stromboli: the article gives the Sicily period as December 1184 to January 1185, not a day, and says only that he saw the volcano. The shipwreck is not placed. Sardinia is an island, not a point; the stop is the sea off its west coast. Alexandria's storm is between Sardinia and Sicily, not at Alexandria; the text puts it before arrival. Granada's entry: places.tsv has only 'Granada'. Article says he went from Granada to Ceuta across the Strait of Gibraltar; the Granada to Ceuta leg is marked land as it is the first stop's set out.
